\section{Trees}

% Generated by scripts/blueprint_from_docstring.py from TCSlib.GraphTheory.Core.Trees.
% Prose is extracted from Lean docstrings; verbatim book quotations are excluded.

\begin{definition}[An edge cut set: a set of edges whose deletion disconnects $G$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsEdgeCutSet}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsEdgeCutSet}
\leanok
Split the vertices into two nonempty groups and collect the edges
running between them; deleting them severs every route from one group to the other.

B\&M define an edge cut \emph{by its shape} $[S, \bar{S}]$; this takes the
operational characterisation --- a subset of \texttt{edgeSet} whose removal leaves $G$
disconnected --- which for \textbf{connected} $G$ describes the same collections.  \textbf{!} For
disconnected $G$ they diverge, and $\emptyset$ satisfies this predicate; that is the source of
the \texttt{IsBond} defect below.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[A bond (\S{}2.2): a minimal (nonempty) edge cut, i.e]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsBond}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsBond}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsEdgeCutSet}
An edge cut with nothing to spare --- remove all of it and the graph falls
apart, but put any single edge back and it is connected again.  Exercise 2.2.8
characterises when $[S, \bar{S}]$ is a bond: exactly when both $G[S]$ and $G[\bar{S}]$ are
connected.  Bonds are the notion \textbf{dual} to cycles, a duality chapter 12 develops in
full --- theorem 2.6 here is the mirror of theorem 2.5.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defect: $\emptyset$ is a bond when $G$ is disconnected.}  The docstring above claims
nonemptiness is automatic because "deleting $\emptyset$ leaves $G$ connected" --- but that holds
only for connected $G$.  For disconnected $G$, \texttt{IsEdgeCutSet $\emptyset$} unfolds to
\texttt{$\lnot$ G.Connected}, which is true, and there is no $B' \subset \emptyset$ to test, so the minimality
clause is vacuous.  Hence \texttt{IsBond G $\emptyset$}, contradicting \emph{minimal \textbf{nonempty} edge cut}.

\emph{The repair:} add \texttt{B.Nonempty} as a conjunct, or carry \texttt{G.Connected} as a hypothesis
wherever \texttt{IsBond} is used (theorem 2.6 already does --- its \texttt{hG} is available).
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The number of spanning trees $\tau(G)$: the number of tree subgraphs $T \le G$ on the full vertex set]
\lean{SimpleGraph.numSpanningTrees}
\label{SimpleGraph.numSpanningTrees}
\leanok
\textbf{!} $\tau(G)$ counts the \emph{distinct} spanning trees, \textbf{not} the
non-isomorphic ones.  B\&M stress the difference: $K_{6}$ has six non-isomorphic spanning
trees (figure 2.1) but $6^{4} = 1296$ distinct ones.  $\tau$ satisfies deletion--contraction
(theorem 2.8) and, for complete graphs, Cayley's formula (theorem 2.9); the general
determinant formula is chapter 12's matrix-tree theorem.

"Spanning" is automatic: a \texttt{T : SimpleGraph W} lives on the whole
vertex type, so \texttt{T $\le$ H $\land$ T.IsTree} already means a spanning tree.  \textbf{!} \texttt{IsTree} bundles
\texttt{Connected}, which requires \texttt{Nonempty W} --- so on an empty carrier $\tau = 0$.  That is
where \texttt{cayley} fails at $n = 0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[contract]
\lean{SimpleGraph.contract}
\label{SimpleGraph.contract}
$G \cdot e$ (\S{}2.4).  Mathlib has no edge contraction for \texttt{SimpleGraph}.
NOTE: a genuine contraction identifies the ends of $e$ and therefore changes the carrier
type (to $|V| - 1$ vertices).  Here it is \emph{stubbed on the same carrier} $V$ as a placeholder,
purely so that the deletion--contraction recurrence (Theorem 2.8) can be typed.

Think of $e = uv$ as a string pulled tight until $u$ and $v$ merge;
everything attached to either is now attached to the merged vertex, and $e$
disappears.  For a link, $\nu(G\cdot e) = \nu - 1$, $\varepsilon(G\cdot e) = \varepsilon - 1$, $\omega(G\cdot e) = \omega$ --- so
contracting an edge of a tree again yields a tree, which is what makes
deletion--contraction work.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective on two counts.}
1. \emph{\texttt{sorry} body.}  $G \cdot e$ is an opaque graph, so theorem 2.8 relates opaque
   quantities and asserts nothing.
2. \emph{Wrong carrier.}  A genuine contraction has $\nu - 1$ vertices; this is stubbed on
   the \textbf{same} carrier $V$ purely so theorem 2.8 can be typed.  Even given an honest
   body on $V$, the identity $\nu(G\cdot e) = \nu - 1$ could not hold.

\emph{The repair} is to move to the quotient carrier ${x : V // x \ne v}$ with $v$'s
incidences re-pointed at $u$, exactly as chapter 10's \texttt{Digraph.contractEdge} does ---
that definition is honest and complete, and can be transcribed.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[tree\_unique\_path]
\lean{SimpleGraph.tree_unique_path}
\label{SimpleGraph.tree_unique_path}
\leanok
A tree has exactly enough edges to hold the vertices together and not one
more: connectivity gives at least one route between any two vertices, acyclicity
forbids a second, since two distinct routes always enclose a cycle.  \textbf{!} The converse
holds for loopless graphs (exercise 2.1.1), so "unique paths between all pairs" is an
equivalent definition of a tree --- that direction is not stated here.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[tree\_card\_edgeFinset]
\lean{SimpleGraph.tree_card_edgeFinset}
\label{SimpleGraph.tree_card_edgeFinset}
\leanok
$\nu - 1$ edges is exactly the price of connecting $\nu$ vertices acyclically
--- corollary 2.4.2 shows it is also the minimum price of connecting them at all.

Stated additively as $\varepsilon + 1 = \nu$ to avoid truncated
$\mathbb{N}$-subtraction.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[tree\_two\_leaves]
\lean{SimpleGraph.tree_two_leaves}
\label{SimpleGraph.tree_two_leaves}
\leanok
A degree-one vertex of a tree is a \textbf{leaf}.  \textbf{!} B\&M offer a more
illuminating alternative (exercise 2.1.2): take a longest path; both endpoints have
degree one, since an extra neighbour would either extend the path or close a cycle.
That route would be shorter in Lean too, if \texttt{exists\_path\_length\_of\_minDegree}-style
machinery from chapter 1 were available.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[cutEdge\_iff\_no\_cycle]
\lean{SimpleGraph.cutEdge_iff_no_cycle}
\label{SimpleGraph.cutEdge_iff_no_cycle}
\leanok
Cut edges are exactly the edges lying on no cycle: an edge on a cycle has
a detour around it, while an edge on no cycle is the sole link between the two sides it
joins.

Mathlib's \texttt{IsBridge} is B\&M's \emph{cut edge}.  Note the conclusion
carries \texttt{G.Adj v w} as a conjunct, which \texttt{IsBridge} includes --- a non-edge is not a
bridge.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[connected\_isTree\_iff\_forall\_edge\_isBridge]
\lean{SimpleGraph.connected_isTree_iff_forall_edge_isBridge}
\label{SimpleGraph.connected_isTree_iff_forall_edge_isBridge}
\leanok
A tree is exactly a connected graph with no redundancy --- every single
edge indispensable for keeping it in one piece.  \textbf{!} Exercise 2.2.1, not stated here,
drops the connectivity hypothesis: $G$ is a \textbf{forest} iff every edge is a cut
edge.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists\_spanningTree]
\lean{SimpleGraph.exists_spanningTree}
\label{SimpleGraph.exists_spanningTree}
\leanok
Keep deleting redundant edges --- those lying on cycles --- until none remain;
what is left still connects everything but has no cycle.  \textbf{*} This is the workhorse of
the rest of the chapter: corollary 2.4.2, theorem 2.6 and corollary 2.7 all open by
invoking it.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[connected\_card\_edgeFinset\_ge]
\lean{SimpleGraph.connected_card_edgeFinset_ge}
\label{SimpleGraph.connected_card_edgeFinset_ge}
\leanok
$\nu - 1$ edges is the minimum price of connecting $\nu$ vertices, and trees
are precisely the connected graphs paying exactly that price.  \textbf{!} Compare exercise
2.1.5, not stated here: for a graph with exactly $\nu - 1$ edges, connected, acyclic and
tree are all equivalent.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[spanningTree\_add\_edge\_exists\_cycle]
\lean{SimpleGraph.spanningTree_add_edge_exists_cycle}
\label{SimpleGraph.spanningTree_add_edge_exists_cycle}
\leanok
A spanning tree already offers a unique route between the ends of $e$;
adding $e$ supplies a second, and the two close off precisely one cycle --- the
\textbf{fundamental cycle} of $e$ with respect to $T$.  \textbf{*} The engine of the exchange
argument for Kruskal's optimality (theorem 2.10), and of chapter 12's tree-basis of the
cycle space.

\textbf{!} Only the \textbf{existence} half is stated: uniqueness of a cycle in
Lean holds only up to rotation and reflection of the walk, which is awkward to phrase
directly.  Chapter 12's \texttt{fundamentalCycle} needs the uniqueness half, so this gap
propagates there.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[cotree\_bond]
\lean{SimpleGraph.cotree_bond}
\label{SimpleGraph.cotree_bond}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsBond}
The exact mirror of theorem 2.5, with \emph{cycle} $\to$ \emph{bond} and *spanning
tree\emph{ $\to$ }cotree*.  \textbf{*} Chapter 12's \texttt{fundamentalBondVertexSet} is exactly the $S$ of
step 3, and cites this theorem by name.

\textbf{!} Both parts consume \texttt{IsBond}, whose $\emptyset$ defect is active
here --- but \texttt{hG : G.Connected} is available as a hypothesis, which is precisely the
condition under which the defect disappears.  Use it explicitly rather than relying on
it silently.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[tree\_isCutVertex\_iff\_degree]
\lean{SimpleGraph.tree_isCutVertex_iff_degree}
\label{SimpleGraph.tree_isCutVertex_iff_degree}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsCutVertex}
In a tree the cut vertices are exactly the internal (non-leaf) vertices.

\textbf{!} Step 2's exercise 2.1.5 is the one real import; Mathlib's
\texttt{IsAcyclic} API may supply it more directly than reproving the book's route.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[connected\_two\_non\_cutVertices]
\lean{SimpleGraph.connected_two_non_cutVertices}
\label{SimpleGraph.connected_two_non_cutVertices}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsCutVertex}
However tangled a connected graph is, there are always at least two
vertices you can delete without breaking it apart.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[numSpanningTrees\_deletion\_contraction]
\lean{SimpleGraph.numSpanningTrees_deletion_contraction}
\label{SimpleGraph.numSpanningTrees_deletion_contraction}
\uses{SimpleGraph.contract, SimpleGraph.numSpanningTrees}
Iterating the recursion reduces any graph to trivial ones and so computes
$\tau$ --- though B\&M note it is impractical for large graphs, which is what motivates
chapter 12's determinant formula.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Currently vacuous.}  \texttt{contract} has a \texttt{sorry} body, so $G \cdot e$ is opaque and this
statement relates opaque quantities.  Worse, \texttt{contract} is a \textbf{same-carrier}
placeholder, so even an honest body on $V$ could not satisfy $\nu(G\cdot e) = \nu - 1$ and step
3's bijection would be false.  Repair \texttt{contract} on the quotient carrier first --- see its
docstring.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[cayley]
\lean{SimpleGraph.cayley}
\label{SimpleGraph.cayley}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.numSpanningTrees}
\textbf{!} B\&M caution that $n^{n-2}$ counts \emph{distinct} spanning trees, not
non-isomorphic ones: $K_{6}$ has six non-isomorphic ones but $6^{4} = 1296$ distinct.

Mathlib has no Cayley formula and no Pr\"ufer correspondence, so all
four steps are from scratch --- the largest single item in the chapter.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists\_min\_weight\_spanningTree]
\lean{SimpleGraph.exists_min_weight_spanningTree}
\label{SimpleGraph.exists_min_weight_spanningTree}
\leanok
Assign each edge a weight and each spanning tree the total; the connector
problem asks for the least, and theorem 2.10 guarantees Kruskal's greedy procedure ---
repeatedly take the cheapest edge not closing a cycle --- always finds one.

\textbf{!} The algorithm is a \emph{procedure}, not a proposition, so what is
stated is the mathematical target it attains: \textbf{existence} of a minimum-weight
spanning tree.  That is strictly weaker than theorem 2.10, which asserts the *greedy
output* is optimal --- the exchange argument quoted above is not exercised by the
skeleton, which is a three-line finiteness argument instead.  Formalising the real
theorem would need Kruskal's algorithm defined first.  Weights are $\mathbb{R}$-valued, matching
B\&M's remark that the algorithm is valid for arbitrary real weights.
\end{theorem}
